key_results: Spectral estimation is formally the problem of using a finite record y(1),…,y(N) from a second-order stationary process to estimate its PSD φ(ω) over −π≤ω≤π. The common practical bottleneck is not computation but the short interval over which stationarity is credible. [§1.5, p. 12]

For a deterministic finite-energy sequence, S(ω)=|Y(ω)|² is the energy spectral density and Parseval gives Σt|y(t)|²=(1/2π)∫S(ω)dω. The same S is the DTFT of the deterministic autocorrelation ρ(k)=Σt y(t)y*(t−k). [§1.2, pp. 3–4]

A zero-mean process is second-order stationary when r(k)=E{y(t)y*(t−k)} depends only on lag. Its autocovariance is conjugate symmetric, r(k)=r*(−k), and |r(k)|≤r(0). Every finite Toeplitz covariance matrix formed from r is positive semidefinite. [§1.3, pp. 5–6]

The first PSD definition is the Wiener–Khinchin transform pair φ(ω)=Σk r(k)e^(−iωk) and r(k)=(1/2π)∫φ(ω)e^(iωk)dω. Consequently r(0), the average signal power, equals the integral of the PSD. [§1.3.1, pp. 6–7]
The second PSD definition is φ(ω)=lim(N→∞)E{|Σ(t=1 to N)y(t)e^(−iωt)|²/N}. It equals the covariance-transform definition when (1/N)Σ(k=−N to N)|k||r(k)|→0. [§1.3.2, pp. 7–8]
A discrete-time PSD is real, nonnegative, and 2π-periodic. It is even for real-valued processes but need not be even for complex processes. [§§1.3–1.4, pp. 8–9]

The authors stress a convention-dependent subtlety: φ(ω) is strictly the spectral content of the chosen autocovariance sequence. Defining covariance with the opposite lag reverses the spectrum, which matters for complex signals. [§1.4, pp. 9–10]
For stationary e(t) passed through an asymptotically stable LTI system H, the output PSD is φy(ω)=|H(ω)|²φe(ω). Complex modulation y(t)=e^(iω0t)x(t) shifts the PSD: φy(ω)=φx(ω−ω0). [§1.4, pp. 10–11]

Nonparametric methods assume no functional form for φ; parametric methods estimate a finite model. Parametric methods can be more accurate when the model is right but are sensitive to misspecification, so nonparametric methods remain competitive even under plausible models. [§1.1, pp. 1–2; §1.5, p. 12]

Complex coherency is Cyu(ω)=φyu(ω)/sqrt(φyy(ω)φuu(ω)). Its magnitude is at most one and weights the least-squares residual power through E|ε|²=(1/2π)∫[1−|Cyu|²]φyy dω. Unit magnitude everywhere means exact mean-square linear dependence. [§1.6.1, pp. 12–13]

The magnitude of coherency is unchanged if y and u are passed through arbitrary stable filters, even different ones. It is therefore the frequency-domain analogue of a scale-invariant correlation coefficient. [§1.6.1, pp. 13–14]
Changing from normalized angular frequency ω to physical angular frequency ω̄=ω/Ts requires a density Jacobian: φ̄(ω̄)=Tsφ(ω̄Ts), not mere argument substitution. [Exercise 1.1, pp. 14–15]

A sequence is a valid ACS exactly when every finite Toeplitz matrix formed from it is positive semidefinite, equivalently when its Fourier transform is nonnegative for every frequency. Simple truncation of a valid ACS can violate this property. [Exercises 1.7–1.8, p. 16]
The Wiener–Hopf relation φyu(ω)=H(ω)φuu(ω) holds both when y is literally the output of H driven by u and when H is the unrestricted LTI filter minimizing E|y−H*u|². [Exercise 1.11, p. 18]
The periodogram drops the unattainable expectation and limit from the second PSD definition: φ̂p(ω)=|Σ(t=1 to N)y(t)e^(−iωt)|²/N. [§2.2.1, p. 22]

The standard unbiased covariance divides a lag-k product sum by N−k; the standard biased estimate divides by N. Despite its name, the biased estimate is usually preferred because high-lag values are damped and the complete sequence is guaranteed positive semidefinite. [§2.2.2, pp. 23–24]

The correlogram computed from the standard biased ACS is exactly the periodogram. This identity connects a squared finite-record transform to the transform of its sample autocovariance and lets both estimators share one analysis. [§2.2.2, p. 24]
An N-point radix-2 FFT uses about (1/2)Nlog2N complex flops versus order N² for direct DFT evaluation; the split-radix comparison quoted is about (1/3)Nlog2N. [§2.3.1, pp. 26–27]

Zero padding samples the same continuous-frequency periodogram more densely. It can reveal the shape between original Fourier bins but cannot improve the estimator’s true spectral resolution. [§2.3.2, pp. 27–28]
MSE decomposes into variance plus squared bias. This decomposition makes clear that a lower-variance refined periodogram may have greater total error if its smoothing bias is too large. [§2.4, p. 28]
The expected periodogram is the true PSD convolved with the Fejér kernel WB(ω)=(1/N)[sin(Nω/2)/sin(ω/2)]², the DTFT of the Bartlett lag window. [§2.4.1, pp. 28–30]

The Fejér main lobe smears neighboring peaks; its sidelobes leak strong-band power into weak or empty bands. The periodogram’s resolution limit is about 1/N cycles per sampling interval, and leakage is especially destructive for large-dynamic-range spectra. [§2.4.1, pp. 30–32]
The periodogram is unbiased for white noise and asymptotically unbiased for a broad class of spectra, but this does not make it a good estimator. [§2.4.1, p. 32]

For circular Gaussian white noise, asymptotic periodogram values at distinct frequencies are uncorrelated, while var{φ̂p(ω)}→φ²(ω). The same result extends to general stable linear processes driven by such noise. [§2.4.2, pp. 32–36]
Because its asymptotic standard deviation equals the PSD itself rather than shrinking with N, the raw periodogram is inconsistent and remains erratic for arbitrarily long records. [§2.4.2, p. 36]

The Blackman–Tukey estimate φ̂BT(ω)=Σ(|k|<M)w(k)r̂(k)e^(−iωk) discards inaccurate high lags and is equivalently a local spectral-window average of the periodogram. Its resolution scales as 1/M and variance as M/N. [§2.5.1, pp. 37–38]

If the lag window is positive semidefinite, so W(ω)≥0, then its Hadamard product with the biased sample covariance remains positive semidefinite and the Blackman–Tukey spectrum is nonnegative. Rectangular lag windows lack this guarantee; Bartlett has it. [§2.5.2, p. 39]

For regular nonnegative window pairs, equivalent duration Ne and bandwidth βe satisfy Neβe=1. Thus window length controls resolution, while M/N controls variance; the stated rule of thumb M≤N/10 reduces standard deviation by at least about three relative to the periodogram. [§2.6.1, pp. 40–41]

At fixed length and w(0), main-lobe and sidelobe energy cannot both be reduced. Window length negotiates resolution versus variance, while window shape negotiates smearing versus leakage. [§2.6.1, p. 41]

For common lag windows, approximate main-lobe width/sidelobe level progresses from rectangular 2π/M and −13 dB through Bartlett/Hann/Hamming near 4π/M and −25/−31/−41 dB to Blackman 6π/M and −57 dB. [§2.6.2, pp. 41–44]

Kaiser γ continuously trades main-lobe width for sidelobe level; Chebyshev makes sidelobes equiripple. Except for Bartlett, the listed fixed windows are not guaranteed to have nonnegative Fourier transforms, but convolving a window with itself creates a positive-semidefinite lag window. [§2.6.2, pp. 41–44]

The leakage-minimizing positive spectral window W=|V|² is obtained by choosing v as the dominant eigenvector of Γ, whose entries are βsinc[(m−n)βπ], then setting w to the autocorrelation of v. This maximizes energy inside |ω|≤βπ. [§2.6.3, pp. 45–47]

A temporal taper v and lag window w=(1/N)(v*v-reversed) produce windowed periodogram and Blackman–Tukey estimators with the same expected spectrum, though not the same realization. [§2.6.4, pp. 47–48]

Bartlett averages L=N/M nonoverlapping M-sample periodograms. Relative to the raw periodogram it reduces both variance and resolution by roughly L, and it is slightly less statistically efficient than a rectangular-window Blackman–Tukey estimate because it discards available lag products. [§2.7.1, pp. 49–50]

Welch improves Bartlett by overlapping segments (commonly 50%) and tapering each before averaging. Overlap supplies more averages; tapering controls bias and downweights shared endpoints, though its variance advantage over Bartlett is usually modest. [§2.7.2, pp. 50–52]

Daniell locally averages periodogram values and is a Blackman–Tukey estimator with a rectangular spectral window and sinc lag window. More zero-padded bins do not create more independent averages: adjacent bins become correlated. [§2.7.3, pp. 52–54]

Periodogram, Blackman–Tukey, Bartlett, Welch, and Daniell are variations on one theme: smooth or average an inconsistent periodogram to reduce variance, necessarily paying with bias or resolution. [§2.8 opening, p. 55]

All N biased sample covariance lags can be computed using a zero-padded FFT, squared magnitudes, and inverse FFT. The rough full-lag crossover favors this over direct order-N²/2 calculation for N at least about 32, subject to implementation details. [§2.8.1, pp. 55–56]

A general windowed Blackman–Tukey estimate needs three FFTs in the presented implementation: two for the sample covariance and one for its windowed transform. An exact discrete spectral-window sum is preferable for special windows such as Daniell’s. [§2.8.2, pp. 57–59]

Apodization chooses a nonnegative, unity-sum temporal window separately for each frequency and dataset by minimizing the fitted sinusoid’s residual output power. Interpreted as a filter, it passes the target sinusoid undistorted and suppresses the other observed components. [§2.8.3, pp. 59–62]

With the one-parameter cosine window, apodization reduces to combining DFT bin k with its two neighbors using a clipped β∈[0,1]. It therefore cuts leakage while retaining periodogram resolution for only marginal extra computation. [§2.8.3, pp. 62–64]
Raw bivariate periodogram coherency is identically one because the 2×2 matrix ZZ*/N has rank one. A meaningful coherency estimate requires spectral smoothing/windowing. [§2.8.4, p. 64]

Cross-covariance need not be even or peak at zero. A short lag window must be centered near its essential lag k0; a poor center either excludes informative lags (bias) or admits noisy high-order lags (variance). [§2.8.4, pp. 64–66]

For broad classes of sequences, generalized duration and bandwidth obey N̄eβ̄e≥1. With energy-variance definitions and mild centering/boundary conditions, Ñeβ̃e≥1/(4π), strengthened by a phase-slope covariance term. [§2.8.5, pp. 66–71]

The book warns that nonparametric time–bandwidth resolution is a limitation of an analysis approach, not necessarily of the signal itself; later parametric methods can resolve structure on scales smaller than 1/Ne when their model is justified. [§2.8.5, p. 68]

For a Gaussian process the exact finite-sample periodogram covariance is |a*(μ)Ra(ν)|²/N². A practical separation exceeding about 4π/N makes two periodogram values nearly uncorrelated; asymptotic independence claims alone conceal this finite-sample scale. [Exercise 2.13, pp. 75–76]

For asymptotically unbiased periodogram estimates with variance φ², multiplying by 1/2 minimizes MSE and halves it—an intentionally stark example in which adding bias improves estimation. [Exercise 2.10, pp. 74–75]
If refined spectral-estimate variance is proportional to φ²(ω), expressing power in dB makes the asymptotic confidence-band width independent of the unknown PSD level. [Exercise 2.12, p. 75]
§3.2, eqs. (3.2.1)–(3.2.4): rational PSDs are dense among continuous spectra and admit spectral factorization φ(ω)=σ²|B(ω)/A(ω)|², with reciprocal-conjugate pole/zero symmetry.
§3.2, eqs. (3.2.5)–(3.2.8): every rational PSD can be realized by filtering white noise through B(z)/A(z); AR, MA, and ARMA are the all-pole, all-zero, and pole-zero specializations.
§3.3, eq. (3.3.4): every ARMA(n,m) covariance sequence obeys r(k)+Σ_{i=1}^n a_i r(k-i)=0 for k>m, the recurrence behind covariance-based AR estimation.
§3.4.1, eqs. (3.4.2)–(3.4.5): the Yule–Walker solution is θ=−R_n^{-1}r_n, and σ² follows from the zero-lag equation; biased sample covariances preserve positive definiteness for any nonzero sample.
§3.4.2, eqs. (3.4.8)–(3.4.10): Yule–Walker is exactly the best linear-prediction solution, with minimum error variance σ_n²=r(0)−r_n*R_n^{-1}r_n.
§3.4.2, eqs. (3.4.11)–(3.4.13): covariance LS minimizes ||y+Yθ||² and gives θ̂=−(Y*Y)^{-1}Y*y; the autocorrelation LS choice is equivalent to Yule–Walker.
§3.4.2: Yule–Walker guarantees a stable estimated AR model, whereas covariance LS may rarely be unstable but is often more accurate at short or medium sample lengths.
§3.5.1, eqs. (3.5.7), (3.5.10), and (3.5.11): Levinson–Durbin updates the order through reflection coefficient k_{n+1}, θ_{n+1}=[θ_n;0]+k_{n+1}[θ̃_n;1], and σ_{n+1}²=σ_n²(1−|k_{n+1}|²).
§3.5.1: Levinson–Durbin obtains all orders through n_max in O(n_max²) work, versus O(n_max⁴) when independent general solves are used for every order.
§3.5.2: Delsarte–Genin exploits real-valued symmetry and is about twice as fast as Levinson–Durbin for real data.

§3.6, eqs. (3.6.2)–(3.6.4): an MA(m) process has r(k)=0 for |k|>m, making its direct covariance PSD estimate identical to a length-(2m+1) rectangular-window Blackman–Tukey estimate; it can be negative.

§3.7.1, eqs. (3.7.1)–(3.7.4): modified Yule–Walker estimates ARMA poles from lags beyond m; overdetermining the system can help narrowband cases when higher-lag covariance signal exceeds estimation noise.
§3.7.1: statistical and numerical accuracy track the condition number of the covariance regression; increasing M is useful only while the added lags improve conditioning and information.
§3.7.1, eqs. (3.7.7)–(3.7.9): after estimating A, the MA covariance polynomial is recovered by filtering the covariance through A; the resulting numerator is not guaranteed nonnegative.

§3.7.2, eqs. (3.7.15)–(3.7.16): two-stage LS first approximates the minimum-phase ARMA process by a high-order AR innovation filter, then regresses on estimated innovations; its PSD is positive by construction.
§3.7.2: the truncation order K controls a bias–variance tradeoff, and zeros near the unit circle require large K, making this a hard case for all ARMA estimators.
§3.8.1, eqs. (3.8.5)–(3.8.6): the multivariate state-space shaping filter is H(z)=z^{-1}C(I−Az^{-1})^{-1}B+I and its spectral density matrix is H(ω)QH*(ω).
§3.8.1, eqs. (3.8.13)–(3.8.19): positive-lag covariances factor as R_k=CA^{k−1}D; P, Q, and B follow from a Riccati equation and algebraic reconstruction.
§3.8.1, eqs. (3.8.20)–(3.8.25): state similarity makes fully parameterized (A,B,C) nonunique; minimality is equivalent to full rank of both observability-like and controllability-like matrices.
§3.8.2, eqs. (3.8.26)–(3.8.31): the block-Hankel covariance matrix factors as R=OC*, has rank n, and its SVD identifies state dimension and subspaces up to a nonsingular transform.

§3.8.3, eqs. (3.8.43)–(3.8.49): practical subspace estimation whitens future/past covariance blocks, chooses model order by the singular-value gap, uses LS/TLS shift fitting for A, and reconstructs P,Q,B.
§3.9.1, eq. (3.9.1): a Levinson reflection coefficient is the negative normalized correlation between forward and backward prediction residuals after intermediate samples have been projected out.

§3.9.2, eqs. (3.9.5)–(3.9.8): admissible next covariance values form an open disk; choosing each disk center sets all subsequent reflection coefficients to zero and yields the maximum-entropy AR extension.
§3.9.3, eqs. (3.9.11)–(3.9.16): Burg recursively minimizes the mean forward/backward error, and Cauchy–Schwarz gives |k̂_p|≤1, hence a stable AR estimate.

§3.9.4, eqs. (3.9.17)–(3.9.22): the Gohberg–Semencul displacement formula determines the entire inverse covariance matrix from the first inverse column despite the inverse generally not being Toeplitz.

§3.9.5, eqs. (3.9.25)–(3.9.31): an invalid negative MA estimate can be projected onto the cone of nonnegative trigonometric polynomials via covariance fitting and a semidefinite quadratic program solvable in polynomial time.
§4.1, eqs. (4.1.6)–(4.1.7): independent uniform phases give r(k)=Σα_p²e^{iω_pk}+σ²δ_{k,0} and φ(ω)=2πΣα_p²δ(ω−ω_p)+σ².

§4.1: high-resolution methods can resolve frequency separations below 1/N cycles/sample because they exploit the exact sinusoidal model, not because the classical Fourier resolution limit is violated without assumptions.

§4.2.2, eqs. (4.2.1)–(4.2.3): A(z)=∏(1−e^{iω_k}z^{-1}) annihilates the noise-free sinusoidal signal; its unit-circle roots encode all frequencies and cannot be canceled from the degenerate ARMA equation.
§4.2.3, eqs. (4.2.5)–(4.2.7): with m≥n and distinct frequencies, the Vandermonde matrix has rank n and R=APA*+σ²I separates a rank-n signal covariance from isotropic noise.
§4.3, eq. (4.3.8): concentrating NLS over complex amplitudes reduces frequency estimation to maximizing Y*B(B*B)^{-1}B*Y, after which amplitudes follow by ordinary LS.
§4.3, eq. (4.3.9): asymptotically Cov(ω̂)=6σ²N^{-3}diag(1/α_k²); under Gaussian white noise this reaches the Cramér–Rao lower bound.
§4.3: NLS remains consistent and asymptotically efficient under unknown colored Gaussian noise when SNR is interpreted locally as α_k²/φ_n(ω_k), unlike the subspace methods.

§4.3, eqs. (4.3.10)–(4.3.17): for one complex sinusoid, the NLS frequency is exactly the largest unwindowed-periodogram peak; for separated multiple lines, the n largest peaks give O(1/N) initial approximations.

§4.4, eqs. (4.4.10)–(4.4.16): the theoretical HOYW covariance matrix has rank n while its sample estimate is full rank; truncating the SVD to rank n both conditions and denoises the estimating equation.
§4.4: increasing L and M supplies more independent low-rank relations but makes higher-lag covariances less reliable and introduces possible spurious noise roots; L+M≈N/3 is suggested.
§4.5, eqs. (4.5.3)–(4.5.13): the smallest m−n eigenvalues equal σ², their eigenvectors span the noise subspace N(A*), and the true frequencies are the only zeros of a*(ω)GG*a(ω).
§4.5, eqs. (4.5.15)–(4.5.18): spectral MUSIC locates pseudospectrum peaks, root MUSIC selects reciprocal roots nearest the unit circle, and Pisarenko is MUSIC with m=n+1.

§4.6, eqs. (4.6.1)–(4.6.14): Min–Norm replaces the full MUSIC noise projector with the unique first-entry-normalized minimum-norm vector in the estimated noise subspace, retaining similar accuracy at lower cost.

§4.7, eqs. (4.7.3)–(4.7.12): deleting the first versus last Vandermonde row gives A_2=A_1D; the eigenvalues of the corresponding signal-subspace LS/TLS map are e^{-iω_k}, yielding ESPRIT frequencies without root sorting.
§4.8, eqs. (4.8.3)–(4.8.14): forward–backward averaging R̃=(R̂+JR̂^TJ)/2 enforces the true covariance’s persymmetry and usually improves short-sample estimation by using more lag products.

§4.8: full Toeplitz averaging is not automatically superior—at finite N and infinite SNR, forward or forward–backward matrices preserve rank n and exact frequencies, while Toeplitz averaging is generally full rank.
§4.9.1, eq. (4.9.1): sample covariances of the random-phase line-spectrum model converge in mean square, which directly supports consistency of covariance-based frequency estimators.
§4.9.2: every positive Toeplitz covariance matrix has a Carathéodory decomposition R=APA*+σ²I with σ² its minimum eigenvalue and n equal to the complementary multiplicity.

§4.9.3, eqs. (4.9.15)–(4.9.17): under white Gaussian noise, sufficiently separated normalized periodogram ordinates are asymptotically independent χ²(2); the maximum yields a detector with prescribed false-alarm risk α.

§4.9.4, eqs. (4.9.20)–(4.9.23): for an arbitrary real time-varying envelope, NLS frequency estimation reduces to the peak of the DFT of y²(t) over [0,π], because squaring moves envelope energy to a nonzero DC component.

§4.9.5, eqs. (4.9.24)–(4.9.31): cyclic minimization and majorization both monotonically descend the objective, but neither guarantees the global minimum; initialization remains decisive for multimodal NLS.
§4.9.6, eqs. (4.9.68)–(4.9.85): frequency-selective ESPRIT projects FFT-band data off a nuisance subspace, retains rank n when M≥m+n, and recommends m=floor(M/2) to maximize independent equations.

§4.9.7, eqs. (4.9.98)–(4.9.121): a 2D sinusoidal sample array admits a linearly parameterized full-row-rank basis for the left null space of its structured data matrix, enabling 2D extensions of modified MUSIC.
Exercise 4.9, eq. (4.10.8): forward–backward symmetrization cannot worsen the condition number: cond(R)≥cond(R+U*R^TU) for Hermitian R and unitary U.

Sec. 5.1 (printed pp. 207–210): assuming the PSD is approximately constant over a fractional-width beta band yields about 1/beta estimable spectral values; consistency requires N beta>1, so increasing beta improves statistical accuracy while degrading resolution.

Sec. 5.2 (printed pp. 210–212): the periodogram is exactly a filter-bank estimator with h_k=(1/N)exp(i omega-tilde k), approximate bandwidth 1/N cycles/sample, and only one power sample per filter—explaining its sharp resolution and persistent variability.

Sec. 5.3.1 (printed pp. 213–216): the length-N unit-energy filter maximizing energy in [-beta pi,beta pi] is the dominant eigenvector of the real symmetric Toeplitz matrix Gamma with entries beta sinc((k-p)beta pi); its eigenvectors are Slepian sequences.

Sec. 5.3.1 (printed pp. 215–216): for large N, Gamma has approximately K=N beta eigenvalues near one and N-K near zero; the K dominant Slepian sequences form the useful orthogonal filter family concentrated in the selected band.

Secs. 5.3.2–5.3.3 (printed pp. 216–223): high-resolution RFB uses beta=1/N and one Slepian output, while stable RFB uses beta=K/N and averages K approximately uncorrelated equal-mean output powers, reducing variance by roughly K at K-fold poorer resolution.
Sec. 5.3.3 (printed pp. 221–223): stable RFB is Thomson's multitaper estimate—an average of K Slepian-windowed periodograms—and is also a rank-K approximation to a Daniell-smoothed periodogram.
Sec. 5.4.1 (printed pp. 223–225): minimizing h*Rh subject to h*a(omega)=1 gives h=R^{-1}a/(a*R^{-1}a) and minimum output power 1/(a*R^{-1}a), the core Capon formula.

Sec. 5.4.1 (printed pp. 225–227): simple bandwidth beta approximately 1/(m+1) produces CM Version 1, (m+1)/(a*Rhat^{-1}a); filter-energy bandwidth produces CM Version 2, (a*Rhat^{-1}a)/(a*Rhat^{-2}a).
Sec. 5.4.1 (printed pp. 226–228): with sliding (m+1)-sample vectors, rank(Rhat)<=N-m, so inversion requires m<N/2; increasing m improves resolution but makes covariance estimation less reliable.

Sec. 5.4.2 (printed pp. 228–231): CM Version 1 is the reciprocal of the arithmetic mean of reciprocal AR spectra of orders 0 through m, explaining its smoother but lower-resolution behavior than a single order-m AR estimate.

Sec. 5.5 (printed pp. 231–235): K=beta N length-N filters constrained to pass K distinct FFT-grid frequencies and null the others have H=A(A*A)^{-1}=A/N; averaging their outputs is exactly the Daniell estimator, and K=1 gives the basic periodogram.

Sec. 5.5 (printed pp. 232–235): when the K filter passbands do not overlap, Gaussian filtered outputs are approximately independent and averaging them reduces PSD-estimate variance by K; K=beta N is the maximum useful filter count.

Sec. 5.6.1 (printed pp. 235–238): reciprocals of order-m AR and Capon spectra are Blackman–Tukey forms; the Capon inverse-covariance sequence is a linearly tapered version of the AR inverse-covariance sequence, hence smoother with poorer resolution.

Sec. 5.6.2 (printed pp. 238–241): Daniell smoothing is exactly a multiwindow method with 2J+1 shifted Fourier tapers; Hanning/Hamming Blackman–Tukey estimates are exact three-taper methods, and a Blackman window gives seven tapers.

Sec. 5.6.3 (printed pp. 241–244): a damped component beta exp((rho+i omega)t) has finite-record energy |beta|^2 exp(2rho)(1-exp(2rho N))/(1-exp(2rho)); Capon-like filtering and LS recovery produce a two-dimensional amplitude/energy spectrum over (rho,omega).

Sec. 5.6.4 (printed pp. 244–247): APES minimizes the LS mismatch between filtered data and beta exp(i omega t) under distortionless response; beta=h*g and h=Qhat^{-1}a/(a*Qhat^{-1}a), with Qhat=Rhat-g g*.

Sec. 5.6.4 (printed p. 247): Capon generally yields slightly better frequency resolution, whereas APES gives much less biased amplitudes; CAPES therefore locates peaks with Capon and evaluates amplitudes with APES.

Sec. 5.6.5 (printed pp. 247–251): GAPES cyclically alternates between a closed-form LS estimate of missing samples and a standard APES update; its nonnegative criterion decreases strictly under weak uniqueness conditions, though convergence may be to a local minimum.

Sec. 5.6.6 (printed pp. 253–254): for rectangular 2D bands, Gamma_2D=Gamma_bar_1D tensor Gamma_1D, so 2D Slepian eigenvalues are pairwise products and eigenvectors are Kronecker products of 1D Slepians.

Sec. 6.2.2 (printed pp. 268–271): narrowband demodulation makes the propagation delay approximately a carrier-phase shift, yielding the snapshot model y(t)=a(theta)s(t)+e(t), and superposition gives y(t)=A s(t)+e(t) for multiple sources.

Sec. 6.2.2 (printed pp. 271–273): for a ULA, a(theta)=[1,exp(-i omega_s),...,exp(-i(m-1)omega_s)]^T with omega_s=2pi d sin(theta)/lambda; avoiding spatial aliasing for arbitrary directions requires d<=lambda/2.

Sec. 6.3.1 (printed pp. 276–278): minimum-norm distortionless spatial weights are h=a(theta)/m, giving conventional beamforming spectrum a*(theta)Rhat a(theta); it is an average of snapshot spatial periodograms.

Sec. 6.3.1 (printed pp. 278–279): conventional beamforming resolution is approximately wavelength divided by array length; it is consistent for one source under white noise but generally inconsistent for multiple finite-aperture sources, especially when close or correlated.

Sec. 6.3.2 (printed pp. 279–280): Capon beamforming minimizes actual output power subject to h*a(theta)=1, giving spatial spectrum 1/(a*(theta)Rhat^{-1}a(theta)); unlike conventional beamforming it allocates nulls to observed interference directions.

Sec. 6.4 (printed p. 281): with spatially white equal-variance noise and nonsingular source covariance, R=A P A*+sigma^2 I; this is the spatial counterpart of the temporal sinusoid covariance model and supports NLS, Yule–Walker, MUSIC, Min-Norm, and ESPRIT.

Sec. 6.4.1 (printed pp. 281–282): concentrating the unknown source snapshots from nonlinear LS gives DOAs maximizing tr(A(A*A)^{-1}A*Rhat); for well-separated directions A*A approximately mI, this decouples into conventional beamformer peaks.

Sec. 6.4.2 (printed pp. 283–284): an off-diagonal covariance block Gamma=Abar P Atilde* has an (L-n)-dimensional null space encoding all DOAs when both partitions exceed n, requiring m>2n but only cross-partition noise decorrelation rather than fully white noise.

Secs. 6.4.3–6.4.5 (printed pp. 284–286): Root MUSIC and Root Min-Norm generally require a ULA; standard MUSIC, Min-Norm, and ESPRIT fail for coherent signals, while ESPRIT additionally requires two identical displaced subarrays satisfying A2=A1 D.

Sec. 6.5.1 (printed pp. 286–288): the asymptotic Min-Norm polynomial factors into n unit-circle signal zeros and m-n-1 noise zeros; minimum coefficient norm makes every noise zero lie strictly inside the unit circle, enabling separation for long samples.

Sec. 6.5.2 (printed pp. 288–289): for a constant-modulus source, concentrated NLS maximizes sum_t |a*(theta)y(t)| rather than the usual sum of squares, with phase estimates arg(a*y(t)) and a closed-form amplitude estimate.

Secs. 6.5.3–6.5.4 (printed pp. 290–298): Capon is equivalently an APES-like stochastic LS fit, an LMMSE/max-SINR filter, or the largest rank-one signal covariance sigma_s^2 a a* that can be subtracted while retaining positive semidefiniteness; this covariance-fitting view admits ellipsoidal steering uncertainty.

Sec. 6.5.4 (printed pp. 296–298): robust Capon reduces to minimizing a*R^{-1}a over the uncertainty ellipsoid; for a spherical set, its unique positive Lagrange multiplier solves a one-dimensional monotone equation after one eigendecomposition.

Sec. 6.5.5 (printed pp. 299–304): diagonal loading is the solution of a constrained Capon problem minimizing h*Rh subject to distortionless response and ||h||^2<=c; feasibility requires c>=1/m, while c below the ordinary Capon noise gain makes the constraint active.

Sec. 6.5.6 (printed pp. 305–312): spatial APES on a ULA aligns overlapping subarrays, minimizes their common waveform residual, and estimates s(t)=h*g(t); choosing subarray length m-1 (two overlaps) maximizes useful filter degrees of freedom.

Sec. 6.5.6 (printed pp. 310–312): by eliminating the signal of interest from the data used to design its filter, APES can reject one coherent interferer and is less sensitive than Capon to small pointing/sample errors, but it loses that advantage with multiple coherent interferers or non-ULA geometry.

Sec. 6.5.7 (printed pp. 312–317): CLEAN repeatedly finds the largest residual beamformer peak and subtracts rho times its point-source beam response; the covariance-fitting error decreases for 0<rho<2, but rho<1 is used to preserve positive-definite residual covariance.

Sec. 6.5.8 (printed pp. 317–319): for i.i.d. circular complex Gaussian snapshots, the unstructured covariance MLE is Rhat=(1/N)sum y y*, while the persymmetric MLE is (Rhat+J Rhat^T J)/2—the forward-backward average.

Exercise 6.2 (printed pp. 320–321): ULA broadside resolution is approximately sin^{-1}(1/L), tending to 1/L radians for large aperture L wavelengths; at arbitrary angle it degrades to approximately 1/(L|cos theta|), becoming poor near end-fire.

Exercise 6.5 (printed pp. 321–322): an arbitrary centered planar array has approximate beamwidth proportional to lambda/D(theta), where D is the RMS projected sensor distance orthogonal to the look direction; this turns array geometry into a directional aperture measure.

Rank is simultaneously the dimension of the column space and row space and the size of the largest nonsingular minor; nonsingular pre- or postmultiplication preserves it, while rank(AB)≤min(rank A,rank B). [A.2, Results R1–R2, printed pp. 329–330; PDF pp. 349–350]
A sum of N outer products has rank at most min(m,N), and premultiplication by a full-column-rank matrix preserves the rank of the following factor. [A.2, Results R3–R4, printed p. 330; PDF p. 350]

Similarity transformations preserve eigenvalues; trace equals the sum of eigenvalues and is cyclic across a conformable two-factor product. [A.3.1, Results R6–R8, printed pp. 331–332; PDF pp. 351–352]
For conformable A and B, |I−AB|=|I−BA| and AB and BA share all nonzero eigenvalues, even when their dimensions differ. [A.3.1, Results R10–R11, printed p. 333; PDF p. 353]
A Hermitian matrix has real eigenvalues and an orthonormal eigenbasis, so A=UΛU*. [A.3.2, Result R12, printed p. 333; PDF p. 353]
The Rayleigh quotient v*Av/(v*v) lies between the smallest and largest eigenvalues of Hermitian A, with equality at the corresponding eigenvectors. [A.3.2, Result R13, printed p. 334; PDF p. 354]

For semiunitary V with n columns, tr(V*AV) lies between the sums of the n smallest and n largest eigenvalues; the extremizing subspaces are spanned by the associated eigenvectors. [A.3.2, Result R14, printed pp. 334–336; PDF pp. 354–356]

For rank-r A=U1Σ1V1*, U1 and V1 span the column and row spaces, while U2 and V2 span the complementary null spaces; dim N(A*)=m−r and dim N(A)=n−r. [A.4, Results R15–R16, printed pp. 336–338; PDF pp. 356–358]
The orthogonal projectors onto R(A) and N(A*) are Π=U1U1* and Π⊥=I−U1U1*=U2U2*. Projector eigenvalues are only zero or one. [A.4, Result R17 and Definition D10, printed pp. 338–339; PDF pp. 358–359]

Truncating the SVD to the p largest singular values gives the best rank-p approximation in Frobenius norm, with squared error Σ_(k>p)σ_k²; it is unique iff σ_p>σ_(p+1). [A.4, Result R18, printed pp. 339–341; PDF pp. 359–361]

Positive (semi)definiteness is equivalently characterized by nonnegative eigenvalues, nonnegative quadratic forms, factorization A=CC*, or principal-minor conditions. [A.5, Definition D11, printed pp. 341–342; PDF pp. 361–362]

A positive semidefinite matrix has infinitely many square roots; the positive semidefinite Hermitian square root is unique, and a positive-definite matrix has a unique Cholesky factor with nonnegative diagonal. [A.5, Definition D12, printed p. 342; PDF p. 362]
The Hadamard product of two positive semidefinite matrices is positive semidefinite. [A.5, Result R19, printed pp. 342–343; PDF pp. 362–363]
If [[A,I],[I,B]] is positive semidefinite and B is nonsingular, then A−B^−1 is positive semidefinite. [A.5, Result R20, printed p. 343; PDF p. 363]
For differentiable positive-definite C(α), ∂ln|C|/∂α=tr(C^−1∂C/∂α), the identity repeatedly used in Gaussian likelihood calculations. [A.5, Result R21, printed pp. 343–344; PDF pp. 363–364]

Cauchy–Schwarz is derived from positivity of a 2×2 Gram matrix for both vectors and integrable functions; equality holds exactly for proportional arguments. [A.5, Results R22–R23, printed pp. 344–345; PDF pp. 364–365]
For distinct nonzero nodes and m≥n, any n consecutive rows of the m×n Vandermonde matrix are linearly independent. [A.6, Result R24, printed pp. 345–346; PDF pp. 365–366]
The block inverse/Schur-complement identities imply the matrix inversion lemma (A−CB^−1D)^−1=A^−1+A^−1C(B−DA^−1C)^−1DA^−1. [A.7, Results R26–R27, printed p. 347; PDF p. 367]
AX=B is consistent iff R(B)⊆R(A), equivalently rank([A B])=rank(A); it has a unique solution iff that holds and A has full column rank. [A.8.1, Results R28–R30, printed pp. 347–348; PDF pp. 367–368]

For a consistent rank-r system, A†=V1Σ1^−1U1* yields the unique minimum-Frobenius-norm solution X0=A†B; all other solutions add a component from N(A). [A.8.1, Result R31 and Definition D15, printed pp. 348–349; PDF pp. 368–369]
Solution sensitivity is governed by cond(A)=σ1/σn. A numerically stable algorithm can still return an inaccurate solution to an ill-conditioned problem. [A.8.1, printed pp. 349–350; PDF pp. 369–370]

For full-column-rank inconsistent AX≈B, the LS solution is (A*A)^−1A*B, but directly forming A*A squares the condition number; QR gives the more stable triangular solve RX=Q1*B. [A.8.2, Result R32, printed pp. 350–351; PDF pp. 370–371]

TLS minimizes perturbations in both A and B. If [A B] has the stated partitioned SVD, X_TLS=−Ṽ21Ṽ22^−1; uniqueness requires a singular-value gap σ̃_n>σ̃_(n+1). [A.8.2, Result R33, printed pp. 352–353; PDF pp. 372–373]
For Hermitian positive-definite A, the unconstrained quadratic F(X)=X*AX+X*B+B*X+C is uniquely minimized at X0=−A^−1B with F(X0)=C−B*A^−1B. [A.9, Result R34, printed pp. 353–354; PDF pp. 373–374]
The linearly constrained minimum of X*AX subject to X*B=C is X0=A^−1B(B*A^−1B)^−1C*. [A.9, Result R35, printed p. 354; PDF p. 374]

For a smooth parametric spectrum, first-order error propagation gives MSE[φ(ω,θ̂)]≈ψ^T(ω,θ)Pψ(ω,θ); parameter-covariance bounds therefore induce frequency-by-frequency spectral MSE bounds. [B.1, equations B.1.1–B.1.4, printed p. 355; PDF p. 375]

The standard CRB bounds covariance of unbiased estimators, but in finite samples it may be unattainable and biased estimators may have smaller MSE; its most persuasive benchmark role is asymptotic, where regular ML estimators attain it. [B.1, printed pp. 356–357; PDF pp. 376–377]

When order is estimated as well as continuous parameters, the large-sample spectral bound becomes an average of order-conditional bounds over Pr(n̂=n); increasing the maximum allowed order increases this error—the price of unknown model dimension. [B.1, equation B.1.10, printed pp. 357–358; PDF pp. 377–378]

For a general differentiable likelihood, P_CR=[E{ss^T}]^−1=−[E{∂²ln p/∂θ∂θ^T}]^−1, where s is the score, and every unbiased estimator satisfies P≥P_CR. [B.2, Result R36, printed pp. 358–359; PDF pp. 378–379]
For real Gaussian data with mean μ(θ) and covariance C(θ), the Slepian–Bangs formula is [P_CR^−1]_ij=(1/2)tr(C^−1C_i'C^−1C_j')+μ_i'^TC^−1μ_j'. [B.3, Result R37, printed pp. 359–361; PDF pp. 379–381]
For circular complex Gaussian data, the compact information element is tr(Γ^−1Γ_i'Γ^−1Γ_j')+2Re{μ_i'^*Γ^−1μ_j'}. [B.3, equation B.3.25, printed pp. 361–363; PDF pp. 381–383]

Under broad congruity/large-sample conditions, the Gaussian CRB is at least as large as the CRB under other distributions with the same mean/covariance; it is therefore a conservative lower-bound benchmark for many second-order methods, though non-Gaussian structure can in principle beat it. [B.3, equations B.3.26–B.3.27, printed pp. 363–364; PDF pp. 383–384]

For line spectra with deterministic phases in circular Gaussian white noise, mean is Vandermonde signal synthesis and covariance is σ²I; exact finite-N CRBs follow from Slepian–Bangs, while a simpler frequency bound is accurate when minimum separation exceeds roughly 1/N. [B.4, printed pp. 364–365; PDF pp. 384–385]

For ARMA models, exact CRB ingredients reduce to autocovariance and cross-covariance computations. The large-sample prediction-error form P_CR,θ={E[ΔΛ^−1Δ^T]}^−1 avoids inverses of matrices whose dimension grows with N. [B.5, equations B.5.5–B.5.6, printed pp. 365–367; PDF pp. 385–387]

For array DOA under deterministic unknown snapshots, CRB_Det(DOA)=σ²/(2N){Re[(D*Π_A⊥D)⊙P̂^T]}^−1; the stochastic-signal model replaces the second factor with one involving PA*R^−1AP. [B.6, equations B.6.32–B.6.33, printed p. 372; PDF p. 392]

With sample signal covariance converging to P, the DOA bounds obey CRB_Sto(DOA)≥CRB_Det(DOA), but they arise from different full data models and only their DOA blocks are meaningfully compared. [B.6, equations B.6.34–B.6.39, printed pp. 372–373; PDF pp. 392–393]

ML under the deterministic-snapshot array model need not attain CRB_Det because the nuisance-parameter count grows with N; ML under the stochastic model satisfies standard fixed-dimension efficiency conditions. [B.6, printed pp. 373–374; PDF pp. 393–394]

Under Gaussian white noise y=μ(γ)+e, ML reduces to NLS: γ̂ minimizes ||y−μ(γ)||² and σ̂²=||y−μ(γ̂)||²/N; the optimized negative log-likelihood is constant+Nlnσ̂². [C.2, equations C.2.5–C.2.8, printed pp. 378–379; PDF pp. 398–399]
For a complex sinusoidal model with N_s samples and n_c components, the real data dimension is N=2N_s and parameter count is n=3n_c+1. [C.2, equations C.2.9–C.2.10, printed p. 379; PDF p. 399]

The MAP model-order rule selects the hypothesis maximizing p_n(y|H_n)p_n(H_n), reducing to maximum marginal likelihood under equal priors; it maximizes total probability of correct detection. [C.3.1, equations C.3.7–C.3.13, printed pp. 382–384; PDF pp. 402–404]

KL discrepancy D(p0,p̂)=E0[ln(p0/p̂)] is nonnegative and vanishes iff p̂=p0; minimizing it is equivalent to maximizing expected model log-likelihood. [C.3.2, equations C.3.15–C.3.19, printed pp. 384–385; PDF pp. 404–405]

Unpenalized maximized likelihood fails completely for nested order families because likelihood is monotone in order and always selects the maximum. The direct-KL ‘no-name’ correction adds penalty n, but still tends to overfit. [C.4, equations C.4.5–C.4.12, printed pp. 386–387; PDF pp. 406–407]

AIC minimizes −2ln p_n(y,θ̂_n)+2n. If a true finite order exists, its underfit probability tends to zero but its overfit probability tends to a positive constant; this same tendency can help approximation when all candidate models are misspecified. [C.5, equations C.5.8 and C.5.12–C.5.13, printed pp. 389–390; PDF pp. 409–410]

For linear regression, AICc replaces AIC’s penalty with [2N/(N−n−1)]n, reducing finite-sample overfit risk at some cost in underfit risk and converging to AIC as N grows. [C.5, equation C.5.15, printed pp. 390–391; PDF pp. 410–411]

With validation data ρ times longer than estimation data, GIC minimizes −2ln p_n(y,θ̂_n)+(1+ρ)n; ρ>1 selects no larger an order than AIC, but no universally optimal ρ exists. [C.6, equations C.6.1–C.6.5, printed pp. 391–392; PDF pp. 411–412]

Under standard information scaling, BIC minimizes −2ln p_n(y,θ̂_n)+nlnN and is asymptotically equivalent to the optimal MAP rule. If information components scale at different rates, the determinant scaling must be recomputed rather than applying nlnN blindly. [C.7, equations C.7.10–C.7.16, printed pp. 394–395; PDF pp. 414–415]
For sinusoids, the information determinant scales atypically and the BIC penalty becomes (5n_c+1)lnN_s, not the generic (3n_c+1)ln(2N_s). [C.7, equations C.7.13–C.7.14, printed p. 394; PDF p. 414]
If the data-generating mechanism is in the tested model class, BIC is consistent: its probability of selecting the correct order tends to one. [C.7, equation C.7.17, printed p. 395; PDF p. 415]

All four criteria share −2ln likelihood+η(n,N)n, with η=2 for AIC, 2N/(N−n−1) for AICc, ν for GIC, and lnN for BIC; the authors’ pragmatic ranking is BIC, GIC with ν=4, AICc, then AIC. [C.8.1, equations C.8.1–C.8.2 and Figure C.1, printed pp. 395–397; PDF pp. 415–417]

Multimodel inference can retain the M best orders and assign normalized weights proportional to exp[−XIC(n_k)/2], interpreting the information criterion as an estimate of twice the negative model log-likelihood. [C.8.2, equations C.8.3–C.8.6, printed pp. 397–398; PDF pp. 417–418]
pedagogy: Stoica and Moses build spectral analysis as a sequence of increasingly structured answers to one ill-posed inverse problem. The opening chapters define PSD from covariance and filtering viewpoints, derive periodogram and correlogram estimators from those definitions, prove their equivalence, and use bias, variance, leakage, and resolution to organize every classical refinement. The parametric chapters begin from generative ARMA or sinusoidal models and proceed through covariance identities, prediction, least squares, subspace geometry, numerical implementation, conditioning, identifiability, and failure modes. Filter-bank and spatial chapters then teach by reinterpretation: each estimator is recast in terms of passband, statistically useful outputs, constrained energy, or array manifold, making clear both the temporal–spatial analogy and where finite aperture, coherence, geometry, or calibration breaks it. Algebraic derivations are compact and proof-forward but repeatedly translated into signal-processing meaning; boxed algorithms make core procedures directly implementable. Complements are substantial research-level extensions rather than decorative notes, covering APES/GAPES, 2D and robust Capon methods, CLEAN, covariance ML, multidimensional/subspace variants, and detailed asymptotic arguments. Exercises mix proofs, counterexamples, algorithm construction, complexity analysis, Monte Carlo experiments, and measured-data studies such as sunspots, lynx counts, Doppler radar, and hydrophone localization. The appendices form a deliberate support course: matrix subspaces and SVD, CRB derivations with finite-sample caveats, and model-order criteria derived from MAP, KL, cross-validation, and Bayesian principles. Throughout, the authors compare statistical accuracy, conditioning, computational cost, identifiability, and model mismatch rather than presenting formulas in isolation. The intended reader is an advanced undergraduate, beginning graduate student, or self-learner already fluent in discrete-time systems, Fourier/z-transform methods, random processes, complex linear algebra, and numerical computation; advanced complements can be skipped on a first pass.

gems: The preface traces ‘spectrum’ from Newton’s prism to the Latin ‘specter,’ then jokes that the student should be a vivid presence rather than a ghostly apparition. [Preface, p. xiii]

One sentence defines the entire field: from a finite stationary record, estimate how total power is distributed over frequency. The wording keeps finiteness and stationarity—often hidden assumptions—front and center. [§1.1, p. 1]

The application roll call spans machine wear, economic cycles, meteorology, astronomy, speech, radar/sonar, ECG/EEG diagnosis, earthquakes and volcanoes, oil exploration, and control-system identification. [§1.1, p. 1]

Complex signals can be simpler than real ones: a real sinusoid is two constrained complex exponentials, while one complex sinusoid is unconstrained and often directly available as I/Q data. [§1.1, pp. 2–3]

The PSD convention caveat is a useful conceptual trap: reversing the autocovariance lag reverses a complex process’s spectrum, so ‘power in the signal at ω’ is not entirely convention-free. [§1.4, pp. 9–10]
Why records stay short even when storage is cheap: the process itself may only be stationary for a short interval. More samples can violate the premise rather than improve the estimate. [§1.5, p. 12]

Coherency is made tangible by regression error: |C(ω)| tells how much of y at each frequency can be explained by a linear filter of u, and remains unchanged under stable filtering of either signal. [§1.6.1, pp. 12–14]

The least-squares FIR spectral approximation exercise reveals a seductive failure: truncating the true covariance minimizes integrated squared spectral error in covariance coordinates, but the truncated sequence may cease to be a valid covariance and produce negative ‘power.’ [Exercise 1.10, pp. 17–18]
The two-sided FFT exercise deliberately invites the wrong ordering, then shows that taking real(fft(z)) can hide a circular-shift error rather than fix roundoff. [Exercise C1.13, pp. 19–20]
A 256×256 covariance matrix’s eigenvalue distribution approaches the distribution of sampled PSD values—an empirical bridge between Toeplitz linear algebra and spectrum. [Exercise C1.14, pp. 20–21]
The periodogram’s historical name comes from Schuster’s 1900 search for hidden periodicities, exactly the task it still visually suggests. [§2.2.1, p. 22]

The ‘biased’ covariance estimate is usually the better scientific object: it behaves at large lags and guarantees a nonnegative periodogram, while the ‘unbiased’ estimate can explode from a single product and yield negative power. [§2.2.2, pp. 23–24]

The periodogram’s failure is summarized as estimating a variance from one filtered sample. Longer records supply more frequencies, not repeated evidence at each frequency, so the fluctuations do not vanish. [§§2.2–2.4, pp. 25, 36]

Zero padding is an interpolation lens, not a resolution microscope: it reveals the already-existing curve between DFT bins but cannot split features the finite observation merged. [§2.3.2, p. 27; Exercise C2.19, p. 80]
Smearing and leakage are separated cleanly: main lobes merge nearby components; sidelobes let strong distant components impersonate weak local power. [§2.4.1, pp. 30–32]

The raw periodogram is asymptotically unbiased yet inconsistent—a memorable warning that bias alone is a terrible quality metric. Its standard deviation approaches the true PSD value itself. [§2.4, pp. 32–36]
The rule M≤N/10 turns an abstract tradeoff into a concrete first move: accept roughly tenfold poorer lag aperture to cut spectral-estimate standard deviation by at least about three. [§2.6.1, p. 41]
The window table makes every designer pay visibly: rectangular gets a 2π/M main lobe but only −13 dB sidelobes; Blackman reaches −57 dB by widening to 6π/M. [§2.6.2, p. 42]

The weak-signal/strong-interferer design example chooses leakage over resolution because the two signals are already well separated. It is a model example of deriving a window objective from the task, not choosing one by habit. [§2.6.3, pp. 45–47]

Welch overlap is not free independent data: tapering the overlapping endpoints partly decorrelates segment estimates, which explains why the practical variance gain is real but not dramatic. [§2.7.2, p. 51]
Daniell’s warning punctures a common zero-padding illusion: averaging more densely sampled bins need not lower variance because those new bins become increasingly correlated. [§2.7.3, p. 53]

Apodization borrows its name from optics—removing the ‘feet’ of a diffraction pattern—and chooses between high-resolution and low-leakage windows at every frequency. In the two-tone example it inherits the best behavior of both. [§2.8.3, pp. 59–64, Figure 2.5]

A raw two-signal coherency estimate is always exactly one, no matter how unrelated the records are, because the unsmoothed outer-product matrix has rank one. This is an exceptionally sharp demonstration of why smoothing is essential. [§2.8.4, p. 64]
The book refuses to oversell the uncertainty principle: the 1/N resolution barrier belongs to nonparametric finite-window filtering, while correct parametric structure can surpass it. [§2.8.5, p. 68]

The shrinkage exercise halves the periodogram before doing anything sophisticated and thereby halves asymptotic MSE—a compact lesson that deliberate bias can beat an unbiased estimator. [Exercise 2.10, pp. 74–75]
Plotting in dB is statistically useful, not cosmetic: when variance scales with φ², log power gives an uncertainty band of constant width across frequency. [Exercise 2.12, p. 75]

The computer sequence moves from controlled two-tone experiments to 50-run Monte Carlo studies and finally to sunspot and Canadian lynx records, asking whether logarithmic detrending makes the lynx cycle more sinusoidal. [Exercises C2.19–C2.23, pp. 80–85]
§3.2, p. 87: rational PSDs are not merely convenient; by Weierstrass they form a dense family for continuous spectra, giving a crisp approximation-theoretic reason for model-based estimation.

§3.4.2, pp. 93–94: the same LS formula becomes either Yule–Walker or covariance LS solely through which boundary rows are included—a concrete illustration of how finite-record conventions change bias and stability.
§3.5, pp. 94–97: narrowband work may test AR orders 50–100; using Toeplitz structure changes the all-orders cost from O(n_max⁴) to O(n_max²), a dramatic algorithmic payoff.
§3.6, pp. 101–103: MA modeling and rectangular-window Blackman–Tukey estimation are shown to be the same assumption in two languages: covariance lags outside ±m are exactly zero.
§3.7.1, pp. 104–105: higher covariance lags are useful only while their slowly decaying signal component dominates estimation noise; this gives an intuitive rule for when overdetermination helps.
§3.7.2, pp. 107–108: the two-stage ARMA method estimates an unobserved innovation by first pretending the process is a high-order AR model—a memorable latent-variable bootstrap.

§3.8.1, pp. 111–113: an infinite family of state-space triples produces the same transfer function via similarity transforms; subspace estimation succeeds by choosing one well-conditioned representative rather than forcing a canonical form.
§3.9.2, pp. 118–119: every next valid covariance lies inside a literal disk in the complex plane, and selecting the center at each step produces the maximum-entropy extension.
§3.9.3, pp. 119–122: Burg turns a multidimensional AR fit into scalar reflection-coefficient updates and proves stability from the elementary inequality 2|c*d|≤c*c+d*d.
§3.9.5, pp. 125–129: the chapter explicitly frames negative PSD repair as ‘factoring the unfactorable,’ then replaces a nonlinear quartic MA fit by convex covariance fitting.
Exercise C3.18, pp. 139–140: two sinusoids at 0.24π and 0.26π with N=64 form a compact super-resolution stress test that exposes resolution, spurious lines, order sensitivity, and pole/zero behavior.
§4.1, pp. 146–147: a line spectrum’s impulses have zero support and finite area 2πα_k²; drawing them as ordinary finite-height peaks obscures the key distinction.

§4.1, p. 148: the authors call the periodogram comparison ‘unfair’ because parametric super-resolution spends exact model information; this is an excellent antidote to magical interpretations of resolution.
§4.3, p. 152: with N=300 and SNR=30 dB, the asymptotic NLS frequency error is about 10⁻⁵, comparable to roundoff in a 32-bit fixed-point processor.

§4.3, pp. 153–155: the maximum of the ordinary periodogram is exactly the NLS solution for one complex sinusoid, and its largest n peaks are principled initializers when lines are separated by more than 2π/N.
§4.4, pp. 157–159: SVD rank truncation is both numerical regularization and statistical ‘noise cleaning’; the same prior rank knowledge solves two problems at once.
§4.5, pp. 161–162: MUSIC’s pseudospectrum is explicitly not a PSD, while Pisarenko is simply the smallest legal MUSIC problem m=n+1—two clarifications often lost in abbreviated treatments.
§4.7, p. 167: ESPRIT avoids pseudospectrum searches and signal/noise root sorting; the authors recommend it as the first choice because its eigenvalues directly carry frequency phases.
§4.8, p. 170: making a covariance estimate fully Toeplitz can destroy exact noiseless finite-sample rank, so enforcing more visible structure can paradoxically make the estimate worse.
§4.9.3, pp. 174–177: an erratic periodogram becomes a formal detector by normalizing its Fourier-grid ordinates, using their χ²(2) law, and thresholding the maximum at a chosen false-alarm risk.

§4.9.4, pp. 177–179: when the amplitude envelope averages to zero, the ordinary DFT has a valley at the carrier; squaring the samples gives the envelope a DC component and creates a peak at twice the carrier.
Exercise 4.1, pp. 198–199: monostatic Doppler radar reduces speed measurement to frequency estimation through ω_D=2ωv/c, directly connecting abstract line spectra to a physical instrument.

Exercises C3.20 and C4.14, pp. 142–143 and 206: the same sunspot and lynx records are revisited with nonparametric, AR/ARMA, and line-spectrum tools, encouraging triangulation rather than allegiance to one estimator.

The chapter makes the periodogram's notorious variability physically obvious: its nominally sharp length-N filter leaves exactly one output sample from which to estimate power. [Sec. 5.2, printed pp. 210–212]

The time-bandwidth product K=N beta is the chapter's master dial: it is simultaneously the number of concentrated Slepian modes, the number of useful nearly independent filter outputs, and approximately the variance-reduction factor. [Secs. 5.3.1–5.3.3, printed pp. 213–223]

Thomson multitaper and Daniell smoothing look unrelated in their usual presentations, but the text makes both into low-rank/filter-bank views of the same band-averaging operation. [Secs. 5.3.3 and 5.5–5.6.2, printed pp. 221–241]

Capon's empirical resolving power can exceed the periodogram's even when a bias-only bandwidth calculation says otherwise; lower random fluctuation can matter more than nominal lobe width. [Sec. 5.4.1, printed pp. 226–228]

The periodogram is re-derived as the solution of a disciplined filter-design problem—minimum white-noise output with one Fourier-bin pass constraint and all neighboring-bin null constraints—so the supposedly crude method is shown to be 'doing well.' [Sec. 5.5, printed pp. 231–235]

APES and Capon form a useful division of labor: Capon tends to localize spectral lines more accurately, while APES avoids Capon's amplitude bias toward zero; CAPES simply assigns each method the job it does best. [Sec. 5.6.4, printed p. 247]

For damped sinusoids, the filter is run backward so the lost m samples come from the low-SNR tail rather than the high-SNR beginning—a small orientation choice with a direct information argument. [Sec. 5.6.3, printed pp. 242–243]

GAPES treats missing samples as optimization variables and assumes only that their spectral content resembles the observed data; the gap fill and spectrum co-evolve instead of interpolation being an invisible preprocessing step. [Sec. 5.6.5, printed pp. 247–251]

The ULA is not merely analogous to temporal sampling: its steering vector is literally a sampled complex sinusoid, turning d<=lambda/2 into a spatial Shannon sampling theorem. [Sec. 6.2.2, printed pp. 271–273]

A fixed physical sensor count cannot grow with the number of snapshots. That simple distinction explains why conventional multi-source beamforming remains asymptotically biased even though related temporal line-periodogram estimates can become consistent as aperture grows. [Sec. 6.3.1, printed p. 279]

Conventional beamforming suppresses every off-look direction equally whether or not energy is present; Capon spends its degrees of freedom only where the observed covariance says interference exists. [Sec. 6.3.2, printed pp. 279–280]

The source-correlation caveat is genuinely spatial: temporal sinusoids at different frequencies have diagonal source covariance, but two emitters can be correlated or fully coherent, breaking standard MUSIC, Min-Norm, and ESPRIT. [Secs. 6.4 and 6.4.3–6.4.5, printed pp. 281–286]

Capon's strength becomes its fragility: a slightly wrong steering vector makes the desired source look like interference, so the adaptive filter dutifully nulls the very signal whose power it was asked to measure. [Sec. 6.5.4, printed p. 294]

Finite-sample covariance error is recast as steering-vector error in a fictitious array model, unifying two apparently different reasons that adaptive beamformers need robustification or diagonal loading. [Sec. 6.5.5, printed pp. 298–299]

Spatial APES designs its filter from a phase-aligned subarray difference in which the desired signal cancels. With one coherent interferer, it can therefore learn to reject the interferer without confusing it with the desired waveform. [Sec. 6.5.6, printed pp. 309–311]

CLEAN's loop gain rho is not merely a cautious heuristic: rho=1 gives the fastest least-squares decrease, but a smaller rho may be necessary to keep every residual covariance physically meaningful and positive definite. [Sec. 6.5.7, printed pp. 313–317]

A single moving sensor becomes a synthetic aperture: after carrier removal, each source direction appears as a Doppler sinusoid with omega_D=-(v omega/c)sin(theta), allowing temporal frequency estimators to perform localization. [Exercise 6.1, printed pp. 319–320]

Near end-fire, a long ULA can still have poor angular resolution because the spatial-frequency map flattens: Delta theta is approximately 1/(L|cos theta|), not simply 1/L everywhere. [Exercise 6.2, printed pp. 320–321]

The measured-data finale asks learners to find submarines in Baltic Sea recordings from only six hydrophones, grounding the entire spatial-spectrum toolkit in an actual surveillance dataset even though the data file itself is external. [Exercise C6.17, printed p. 327]

The proof of |I−AB|=|I−BA| uses two three-factor block-matrix products whose left sides have the same determinant; the identity then immediately yields the shared nonzero eigenvalues of AB and BA. [A.3.1, Results R10–R11, printed p. 333; PDF p. 353]

The authors call best low-rank approximation a result that ‘even alone would be enough to make the SVD an essential matrix analysis tool,’ then prove it rather than merely cite Eckart–Young. [A.4, Result R18, printed pp. 339–341; PDF pp. 359–361]

A clean numerical warning turns an innocent formula into a practical lesson: evaluating LS through (A*A)^−1A* squares the condition number, so the mathematically correct normal equations can be computationally unwise. [A.8.2, printed p. 351; PDF p. 371]

LS and TLS are distinguished by a memorable modeling question: is only B noisy, or are both A and B perturbed? The two answers lead respectively to projection/QR and augmented-matrix SVD. [A.8.2, printed pp. 350–353; PDF pp. 370–373]
The CRB chapter begins by warning against ritual comparison: at small N the bound may be unattainable, and a biased estimator can have MSE below the unbiased CRB. [B.1, printed p. 356; PDF p. 376]

Unknown order has an explicit statistical price: average the conditional spectral bounds over the limiting order-selection probabilities, and the bound rises as the maximum candidate order expands. [B.1, printed pp. 357–358; PDF pp. 377–378]

The Gaussian CRB is framed as a broadly conservative benchmark: with matching mean/covariance, other distributions can carry extra exploitable information and therefore admit smaller bounds. [B.3, printed pp. 363–364; PDF pp. 383–384]

The array discussion shows a subtle failure of the familiar ‘ML attains CRB’ slogan: deterministic unknown snapshots add O(N) nuisance parameters, so the parameter-to-data ratio does not vanish. [B.6, printed pp. 373–374; PDF pp. 393–394]

After deriving deterministic and stochastic array models, the authors advise treating the assumptions as instruments for deriving algorithms, not as a metaphysical choice: use MLDet for simplicity or MLSto for greater accuracy regardless of the literal signal origin. [B.6, printed p. 376; PDF p. 396]

The unpenalized nested-model rule is not merely imperfect—it ‘fails completely’ by always choosing the maximum allowed order. This makes the need for information-criterion penalties unavoidable. [C.4, printed p. 386; PDF p. 406]

The first corrected KL penalty is deliberately called the ‘no-name’ rule. Its penalty n is enough to improve on raw likelihood but not enough to prevent overfitting, preparing the logic for AIC’s 2n. [C.4, printed pp. 386–387; PDF pp. 406–407]

AIC’s inconsistency is not presented as pure defect: when reality is more complex than every tested model, its willingness to select larger orders can improve approximation and prediction. [C.5, printed p. 390; PDF p. 410]

GIC gets an intuitive cross-validation story: make the validation sample longer than the estimation sample, and a model that learned the estimation noise has more opportunity to fail. [C.6, printed pp. 391–392; PDF pp. 411–412]

BIC’s claim to fundamentality comes from converging derivations: KL with an N-independent prior, full Bayesian marginal likelihood/MAP, and minimum description length all lead to the same logarithmic penalty form. [C.7, printed pp. 392–395; PDF pp. 412–415]

The sinusoid example catches a common plug-in error: Fisher information for frequency grows at a different rate, so generic nlnN parameter counting gives the wrong BIC penalty. [C.7, printed p. 394; PDF p. 414]
Figure C.1 makes the criteria’s personalities visible: AIC stays flat at 2, GIC ν=4 stays flat at 4, AICc falls toward 2, and BIC keeps growing as lnN. [C.8.1, Figure C.1, printed p. 397; PDF p. 417]

The final model-selection move avoids throwing away near-winners: exp(−XIC/2) converts criterion differences into normalized likelihood-style weights for a small ensemble. [C.8.2, printed pp. 397–398; PDF pp. 417–418]

One selected exercise answer gives a concrete warning that an ‘unbiased’ autocovariance sequence need not yield a nonnegative spectral estimate: y={1,1.1,1} produces a specified trigonometric estimate that can violate PSD validity. [Appendix D, answer 2.3, printed p. 399; PDF p. 419]

The reference apparatus is more than a bibliography: nonparametric, rational, line, and spatial literatures are split into historical/classical/recent strata, giving a ready-made research reading ladder. [References Grouped by Subject, printed pp. 415–419; PDF pp. 435–439]
